why: no model has been rendered and compared with the unit
claim: This type is eight peaking sections parked at fixed centres, one output pan and one level, with a single width byte driving all eight instead of one each. The centres are the named third octaves at 250, 500, 1k, 1.25k, 2k, 3.15k, 4k and 8k: a band raised to the top of its byte and cut to the bottom returns the same centre to within 0.02 octaves, and the eight sit 0.030 octaves under the named series with a scatter of 0.018 -- which is the offset this unit's other equaliser's table was measured to carry. That offset has since been measured to be the unit's rather than the reading's, by putting a section of known centre through the same band set, window and fit at the width both types were read at, where it comes back on the name to two thousandths of an octave -- so the eight really do sit below the series they are named by. With each type's own mean taken out the seven centres the two types share still run the same way, over a pattern 0.046 octaves wide that they disagree about by 0.012 at worst and 0.006 in the median. Whether that is one table or two tables computed the same way is not separated here. The width byte indexes five entries and four of them are the equaliser's Q byte's entries exactly: 2.583, 1.417, 0.750 and 0.417 octaves between the half-gain points, on a reading whose step is a twelfth. Past the fifth printed step the two types disagree. This one returns the fifth entry and the equaliser returns the first, so what is shared is the table and not the handling of a byte outside it. Each band gain answers over the twenty-five values from 52 to 76 and returns the nearest end for everything outside, and the power-on state is the eight defaults its own page prints, read through a width byte the page prints no default for and which powers up at its third entry.
named: The eight band gains at 40 03 03 through 40 03 0A, the width byte at 40 03 0B and the pan at 40 03 15, on type 01 01.
adds: Three standing claims reach this type for the first time and one of them is cut back. The gain class claim and the width claim did not name 01 01 at all; the pan class claim named it and had never been held against a record on it. What is new beyond that reach is the structure: eight sections at fixed centres is not a shorter equaliser, it is the same sections with the frequency byte removed and replaced by a position in the table, and one width byte serving all eight rather than one per section is the arrangement that makes eight sections cost what four did. The cut is to the width claim, whose rule for a byte past the printed steps holds on the type it was fitted on and not on this one.
refutedBy: A band whose raised and cut takes disagree about its centre by more than the spread the other seven show, which would mean the eight are not fixed sections but something whose position moves with its gain. A width setting whose half-gain span differs from the equaliser's at the four entries the band set contains by more than the twelfth of an octave the reading steps in. A gain byte answering outside 52 to 76.
whatItWouldChange: Two class claims gain a type and one is cut back. A renderer for this type is eight of the sections the equaliser claim already describes, at seven of the entries the frequency claim already lists and one above them, behind one shared width -- so nothing new has to be modelled for it beyond the fixed positions. And the width claim's rule for a byte past its printed steps becomes a property of the type rather than of the byte, which is the kind of thing a renderer gets wrong silently because no setting a musician uses reaches it.

eraPriors.claim: A graphic equaliser of this period shares one width across its sections rather than giving each its own.
eraPriors.why: A section's coefficients are recomputed when its width moves. One shared width is one recomputation for eight sections and one byte of state; eight widths are eight of each, which is what makes eight sections cost more than twice what four do.
eraPriors.wouldBeWrongIf: The page printed a width per band, or the one it prints moved some bands and not others. It prints one, and the one it prints returns the same five entries this unit's parametric equaliser returns from its own per-section width byte -- so the sharing is in how many bytes there are, not in a cheaper filter.

alternatives.reading: The eight centres are the named third octaves themselves, and the 0.030 octaves both this type and the equaliser's table sit under them is carried by the reading rather than by the unit.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: The reading was measured to return a known centre at the width both types were read at: a mean of +0.0001 octaves over the eight with a scatter of 0.0019, against a term of 0.030. Nothing is left for the reading to carry.

alternatives.reading: The width byte is not written above its fifth printed step, so what the high settings return is whatever the type was already holding.
alternatives.ruledOutBy: The type powers up with that byte at its third entry, which this run measured rather than assumed -- the takes with nothing written return the third step's profile to a tenth of a decibel across twenty-two bands. A refused write would therefore leave 1.417 octaves between the half-gain points. Bytes five, sixty-four and a hundred and twenty-seven all return 0.417, which is the fifth entry. The write is taken and held at the top of the table.

alternatives.reading: The eighth band is past the end of the table, rather than past what four bits of a frequency byte can reach of it.

separatedBy.observable: Where a table entry above 6.3k sits, asked through a byte that indexes the table rather than through a section parked at one of its entries.

predicts.the table ends at the sixteenth entry: nothing indexes an entry above 6166.8, and the eighth band is a section placed outside the table
predicts.the table is longer than four bits reach: an entry near 7900 exists and something indexes it

separatedBy.sensitivity_here: Not a question of resolution. The eighth band sits 0.36 octaves above the highest entry the equaliser's byte returns, which is twenty times the scatter of the eight and far outside any reading's own spread. What is missing is a byte to ask with.
separatedBy.why_not_separable: No byte in the printed tables indexes a peaking centre above 6.3k. The equaliser's own high corner prints 4k and 8k, but it is a two-state shelf and what it moves is where a slope runs steepest -- 9.5k against 11.3k between its two states, with the profile still rising at the top of the band set in both. That says where a shelf hinges and not where a table entry sits, so it cannot be held against a centre. Until a type is found whose frequency byte reaches past 6.3k, a seventeenth entry and a section outside the table predict the same eight numbers, and this is a margin of one -- the bar this project refuses to queue below.

extra.text: Whether the centres are entries of one shared table or two uses of one named series, which is the standing alternative and costs nothing to settle. What the level byte does, which was not asked. Whether the eight sections are in a chain or summed in parallel: a band profile is magnitude and eight sections at 0 dB are unity either way, which is also why the flat reference this run measured against is the same reference under both. The pan byte's table, which five settings cannot count -- what they say is that its centre sits 2.67 dB under its end, neither the 3.01 of a constant-power pair nor the 6.02 of a crossfade, and that is one figure of a table the pan claim reads nineteen entries in.

The prediction was written before the unit was booked and names what each of the four claims reaching this type would have to return. Two parts of it were wrong and the record of that is worth more than the parts that landed. The width claim's rule for settings past the printed steps was predicted to hold and it does not. And the page's eight printed defaults were predicted to be what the type powers up holding, which they are -- but the prediction could not say what depth they would be read at, because the width byte they are read through is printed as a list with no middle and so has no printed default. That gap was written down before the run and is why the power-on gains were taken again through each of the five widths, which is what put the byte's own default at the third entry.
